concepts.name: Meaning, classification and ad hoc committees
concepts.description: What makes a body a parliamentary committee, standing versus ad hoc committees, the six categories, select and joint committees on Bills, and consultative committees.
concepts.idea: A parliamentary committee works under the Speaker/Chairman and reports to the House, and committees are standing or ad hoc.
concepts.rule: The Constitution mentions committees but leaves their composition, tenure and functions to the rules of the two Houses (p.394). A parliamentary committee is appointed or elected by the House or nominated by the Speaker/Chairman, works under his direction, reports to the House or to him and has a secretariat from the Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha; consultative committees fail these conditions (p.394). Standing committees are permanent and fall into six categories, while ad hoc committees are temporary and are inquiry or advisory committees (pp.394-396). Select and joint committees on Bills are the advisory committees; the motion is moved and adopted in the House where the Bill is under consideration, and the Committee takes evidence, goes clause by clause and may carry notes of dissent (p.396). Consultative committees are chaired by the minister in charge, constituted by the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs, have 10 to 30 members and stand dissolved with each Lok Sabha (p.408).
concepts.example: A select committee examining a Bill clause by clause and hearing experts is an advisory ad hoc committee; the Committee on Papers Laid on the Table is a standing committee that scrutinises and controls.

concepts.name: Public Accounts Committee
concepts.description: Origin, composition, chairman, functions with the CAG's reports, and the limitations of the Public Accounts Committee.
concepts.idea: The Public Accounts Committee examines the CAG's audit reports and the Union's accounts after the money has been spent.
concepts.rule: The committee was first set up in 1921 under the Government of India Act of 1919 and now has 22 members, 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha, elected every year by the single transferable vote; a minister cannot be a member (p.396). The Speaker appoints its chairman, and since 1967 by convention he is from the Opposition (p.396). It examines the CAG's audit reports, the appropriation and finance accounts, the accounts of state corporations and autonomous bodies audited by the CAG, and excess expenditure over grants, checking economy, prudence and propriety (p.397). The CAG is its guide, friend and philosopher (p.397). It conducts a post-mortem, does not decide policy, cannot disallow expenditure or issue orders, and its recommendations are advisory (p.398).
concepts.example: The committee finds that a department spent more on a service than the Lok Sabha had granted and reports on it, but only Parliament can decide what to do.

w: That is how the Department-Related Standing Committees are filled.
The chapter prescribes proportional representation, so that all parties get due representation.
The members are elected by Parliament.

concepts.idea: The Estimates Committee suggests economies in the budget estimates while the Committee on Public Undertakings reviews how public undertakings are run.
concepts.rule: The first post-independence Estimates Committee was constituted in 1950 on John Mathai's recommendation; its 25 members became 30 in 1956, all from the Lok Sabha, elected every year, with the chairman generally from the ruling party (p.398). The Committee on Public Undertakings was created in 1964 on the Krishna Menon Committee's recommendation with 15 members, raised to 22 (15 Lok Sabha, 7 Rajya Sabha) in 1974 (p.399). It examines the reports and accounts of public undertakings and whether they follow sound business principles, but not major policy, day-to-day administration or matters under a special statute, and not more than ten to twelve undertakings a year (pp.399-400).

concepts.idea: The 24 Department-Related Standing Committees scrutinise ministries' demands for grants, bills and reports to make the executive more accountable.
concepts.rule: Seventeen DRSCs were set up in 1993 on the Rules Committee of the Lok Sabha's recommendation and seven more in 2004 raised the number to 24; eight work under the Rajya Sabha and sixteen under the Lok Sabha (pp.400, 403). Their objective is greater accountability of the Executive, especially financial (p.400). Each has 31 members (21 Lok Sabha, 10 Rajya Sabha), nominated by the Speaker and the Chairman; a minister is not eligible and the term is one year (p.400). They consider demands for grants (without suggesting cut motions), bills, annual reports and long-term policy documents, but not day-to-day administration, and their recommendations are advisory (pp.403-404). concepts.name: Committees to inquire, scrutinise and control
concepts.description: Committees on Petitions, Privileges, Ethics, Government Assurances, Subordinate Legislation, Papers Laid, SC/ST welfare, Empowerment of Women and Offices of Profit.
concepts.idea: Each inquiry or scrutiny committee has a distinct task, such as ministers' promises, delegated legislation or disqualification for offices of profit.
concepts.rule: The Committee on Petitions examines petitions on bills and matters of public importance, the Committee of Privileges is semi-judicial, and the Ethics Committee, constituted in 1997 in the Rajya Sabha and in 2000 in the Lok Sabha, enforces the code of conduct (p.405). According to the chapter, the Committee on Government Assurances (1953) follows up ministers' promises, the Committee on Subordinate Legislation (1953) checks delegated rule-making, and the Committee on Papers Laid on the Table (1975) checks papers against the Constitution, Act or Rule but leaves statutory notifications to the Subordinate Legislation committee (p.406). The SC/ST welfare committee and the Committee on Empowerment of Women (1997) have 30 members each, 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha (p.406). The Joint Committee on Offices of Profit has 15 members and recommends disqualification (p.406).
concepts.example: If a minister promises in the House to start a scheme, the Committee on Government Assurances later reports how far the promise was kept.
